title: Keep the faster types honest
teaser: A small compile-time guard catches the expensive default creeping back in.

blocks.text: We made “no global field omissions” a testable contract. The client options prohibit configuring `omit` with `omit?: never`; a compile-time guard checks that the resulting clients still carry `undefined` for global omission after extensions are applied.

blocks.label: Focused excerpt from our type regression test
blocks.code:
import { expectTypeOf, it } from "vitest"
import type { PrismaClient } from "./generated/prisma/client"
import type { prisma, basePrisma } from "./prismaClient"

type GlobalOmitOf<T> =
    T extends PrismaClient<infer _Log, infer GlobalOmit>
        ? GlobalOmit
        : never

it("keeps global omission undefined", () => {
    expectTypeOf<
        GlobalOmitOf<PrismaClient<never, { user: { email: true } }>>
    >().toEqualTypeOf<{ user: { email: true } }>()
    expectTypeOf<GlobalOmitOf<typeof prisma>>().toBeUndefined()
    expectTypeOf<GlobalOmitOf<typeof basePrisma>>().toBeUndefined()
})

blocks.text: The first expectation proves the helper can extract an actual omission map. The next two catch the global-omit type widening again, including through an extension boundary. Our full test covers the integration clients too. Include this file in the compiler check: running Vitest alone does not validate these type expectations.

That guard protects the type contract, not database behavior. We also ran the relevant transaction and numbering tests and compared emitted JavaScript: all eight changed implementation files were identical. The `undefined` here is a type argument; it does not remove fields at runtime.

Revisit the guard when enabling global omission or upgrading Prisma. This excerpt uses our generated client’s type alias with two explicit type arguments; its constructor has a different signature. Inspect your generated types before copying it. If the configuration changes, update the contract with it.
